arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Summa argued that prior convictions lacked the necessary mental state element.
Mr. Bond argued that the statutory text does not require a generic crime comparison.
Justice Alito questioned the existence of a mens rea element in the Florida defense.
Justice Ginsburg questioned the prosecution's burden regarding the defendant's knowledge of the substance.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case asks if a state drug offense that does not require proof of guilty knowledge counts as a serious crime for federal sentencing enhancements.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the court to exclude prior state drug convictions that lack a knowledge element from federal sentencing enhancements.
The government wants the court to include prior state drug convictions as serious offenses regardless of the knowledge element.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that state drug laws without a guilty knowledge requirement do not match the generic definition of a serious crime.
The government argues that the statutory text does not require a generic analogue inquiry for this specific sentencing provision.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Alito asked if the defendant could have raised an affirmative defense regarding the substance identity.
Justice Ginsburg asked if the prosecution must prove the defendant knew the substance was cocaine if the defendant claimed ignorance.
